title: Chapter 11 — That The Equality Of Conditions Contributes To The Maintenance Of Good Morals In America
paragraphs: Maintenance of Good Morals in America

Some philosophers and historians have claimed, or hinted, that the strictness of women’s morals rises or falls simply with a country’s distance from the equator. That was an easy answer: all it took was a globe and a pair of compasses to settle in an instant one of the hardest problems of human life. But I know of no facts that support this doctrine of the materialists. The same nations have been chaste at one time in their history and dissolute at another. So the strictness or laxity of their morals must have depended on some cause that changes, and not only on the natural features of their country, which never changed. I do not deny that in certain climates the passions arising from the mutual attraction of the sexes are unusually intense. But I believe that this natural intensity can always be stirred up or held in check by the condition of society and by political institutions.

Travelers who have visited North America disagree on a great many points, yet they all remark that morals there are far stricter than anywhere else. On this point the Americans are clearly far superior to their ancestors, the English. A superficial glance at the two nations is enough to establish it. In England, as in every other country of Europe, public malice is forever attacking the frailties of women. Philosophers and statesmen can be heard lamenting that morals are not strict enough, and the country’s literature constantly suggests as much. In America every book, novels included, takes women to be chaste, and no one thinks of telling tales of gallantry. No doubt this great regularity of American morals comes partly from the country, from the race of its people, and from their religion. But these causes, which operate elsewhere too, are not enough to account for it; some special reason must be found. That reason seems to me to be the principle of equality and the institutions that follow from it. Equality of conditions does not by itself produce regularity of morals, but it undoubtedly makes it easier and increases it. *a [Footnote a: See Appendix T.]

Among aristocratic nations, birth and fortune often make man and woman such different beings that they can never be joined to each other. Their passions draw them together, but the condition of society and the ideas it suggests keep them from forming a lasting and public bond. The inevitable result is a great number of brief, secret liaisons. Nature quietly takes revenge for the restraint that human laws place on her. It is much less so when equality of conditions has swept away all the barriers, imaginary or real, that separated man from woman. No girl then believes that she cannot become the wife of the man who loves her, and this makes any breach of morality before marriage very uncommon. For however credulous the passions may be, a woman can hardly persuade herself that she is loved when her lover is perfectly free to marry her and does not.

The same cause works, though more indirectly, on married life. Nothing does more to justify an illicit passion, in the eyes of those who feel it and of the world that watches, than a forced or accidental marriage. *b In a country where a woman is always free to exercise her power of choice, and where her education has prepared her to choose well, public opinion shows her faults no mercy. The strictness of the Americans comes in part from this. They regard marriage as a covenant that is often burdensome, but one whose every condition the parties are strictly bound to fulfill, because they knew all those conditions beforehand and were perfectly free not to enter into it.

[Footnote b: The literature of Europe amply confirms this remark. When a European author wants to portray in a work of imagination one of those great catastrophes of married life that happen so often among us, he takes care to win the reader’s sympathy by showing him ill-matched or forced marriages. Long-standing tolerance has relaxed our morals, yet an author could hardly interest us in the misfortunes of his characters if he did not first excuse their faults. This device seldom fails, because the scenes we see every day have prepared us long in advance to be indulgent. But American writers could never make such excuses believable to their readers. Their customs and laws are against it, and since they despair of making loose conduct appealing, they stop depicting it. This is one of the causes to which the small number of novels published in the United States must be attributed.]

The very circumstances that make marital fidelity more of a duty also make it easier. In aristocratic countries the aim of marriage is to unite properties rather than persons; so the husband is sometimes still at school and the wife still with her nurse when they are betrothed. It is no wonder that the conjugal tie, which holds the couple’s fortunes together, lets their hearts wander. That is the natural result of the nature of the contract. When, on the contrary, a man always chooses his wife for himself, with no outside compulsion or even guidance, it is generally a likeness of tastes and opinions that brings a man and a woman together, and the same likeness keeps them close and settles them in habits of intimacy.

Our forefathers had formed a very strange idea about marriage. They had noticed that the few love matches of their day almost always turned out badly, and they firmly concluded that it was exceedingly dangerous to follow the dictates of the heart in this matter. Chance seemed to them a better guide than choice. Yet it was not hard to see that the examples they witnessed proved nothing at all. In the first place, if democratic nations leave a woman free to choose her husband, they take care to give her mind enough knowledge and her will enough strength to make so important a choice. The young women of aristocratic nations, by contrast, who slip away secretly from their parents’ authority and throw themselves of their own accord into the arms of men they have had neither the time to know nor the ability to judge, are wholly without those safeguards. It is not surprising that they misuse their freedom of action the first time they take it, nor that they fall into such cruel mistakes when, having had no democratic education, they choose to marry according to democratic customs. But that is not all. When a man and a woman are set on marrying despite the differences of an aristocratic state of society, the difficulties to be overcome are enormous. Having broken or loosened the bonds of filial obedience, they must then free themselves by one last effort from the sway of custom and the tyranny of opinion. And when at length they have accomplished this arduous task, they find themselves estranged from their natural friends and kinsmen: the prejudice they have defied separates them from everyone and puts them in a situation that soon breaks their courage and sours their hearts. If a couple married in this way are first unhappy and later guilty, then, this should not be blamed on the freedom of their choice but on their living in a community where that freedom is not admitted.

Moreover, we should not forget that the same effort that makes a man violently throw off a prevailing error usually carries him past the bounds of reason. To dare to declare war, however just the cause, on the opinion of one’s age and country takes a violent and adventurous spirit, and men of that character seldom reach happiness or virtue, whatever path they follow. This, incidentally, is why in the most necessary and righteous revolutions it is so rare to find virtuous or moderate revolutionary figures. There is therefore no good reason for surprise if a man who, in an age of aristocracy, consults nothing but his own opinion and taste in choosing a wife soon finds breaches of morality and domestic misery invading his household. But when this same course of action belongs to the natural and ordinary order of things, when it is sanctioned by parental authority and backed by public opinion, there can be no doubt that it will increase the inner peace of families and make conjugal fidelity more strictly observed.

Almost all men in democracies are engaged in public or professional life; and meanwhile the modest size of ordinary incomes obliges a wife to stay at home and watch over the details of domestic economy in person and very closely. All these separate and compulsory occupations are so many natural barriers. By keeping the two sexes apart, they make the advances of the one less frequent and less ardent, and the resistance of the other easier.

Not that equality of conditions can ever succeed in making men chaste, but it may give their breaches of morality a less dangerous character. Since no one then has enough time or opportunity to assail a virtue that is armed in its own defense, there will be, side by side, a great number of courtesans and a great number of virtuous women. This state of things causes lamentable cases of individual hardship, but it does not keep the body of society from being strong and alert. It does not destroy family ties or weaken the morals of the nation. Society is endangered not by the great profligacy of a few, but by laxity of morals among all. In the eyes of a legislator, prostitution is less to be feared than intrigue.

The restless, ceaselessly harried life that equality makes men lead not only distracts them from the passion of love, by leaving them no time to indulge it, but also turns them away from it by another road, more hidden but more certain. All men who live in democratic ages take on, to some degree, the ways of thinking of the manufacturing and trading classes. Their minds take a serious, deliberate, and practical turn. They tend to give up the ideal in order to pursue some visible, nearby object that seems the natural and necessary aim of their desires. Thus the principle of equality does not destroy the imagination, but it lowers its flight to the level of the earth. No men are less given to reverie than the citizens of a democracy, and few of them are ever known to yield to those idle, solitary musings that usually precede and produce the great emotions of the heart. It is true that they set great store by obtaining for themselves the kind of deep, steady, quiet affection that is the charm and safeguard of life. But they are not inclined to chase after those violent and capricious sources of excitement that disturb it and cut it short.

I am aware that all this applies in its full extent only to America and cannot at present be extended to Europe. Over the last half-century, while laws and customs have driven several European nations toward democracy with unprecedented force, we have had no occasion to observe that the relations between man and woman have become more orderly or more chaste. In some places one may detect the very reverse: some classes are stricter, while the general morality of the people appears laxer. I do not hesitate to say so, for I am as little inclined to flatter my contemporaries as to slander them. This fact must distress us, but it ought not to surprise us. The favorable influence that a democratic state of society may have on orderly habits is one of those tendencies that can only be discovered after some time. If equality of conditions favors purity of morals, the social upheaval by which conditions are made equal works against it. During the last fifty years, in which France has been going through this transformation, that country has rarely had freedom and always had disturbance. Amid this universal confusion of ideas and general stir of opinions, amid this incoherent mixture of the just and the unjust, of truth and falsehood, of right and might, public virtue has become doubtful and private morality unsteady. But all revolutions, whatever their aim or their agents, have at first produced similar consequences; even those that in the end drew the bonds of morality tighter began by loosening them. The violations of morality that the French so often witness do not seem to me permanent, and some curious signs of the times already point that way.

Nothing is more wretchedly corrupt than an aristocracy that keeps its wealth after it has lost its power, and that still has a great deal of leisure after being reduced to ordinary, vulgar pastimes. The energetic passions and great conceptions that once animated it then leave it, and nothing remains but a swarm of petty, consuming vices that cling to it like worms on a carcass. No one denies that the French aristocracy of the last century was extremely dissolute, whereas established habits and ancient belief still preserved some respect for morality among the other classes of society. Nor will anyone dispute that today the remnants of that same aristocracy show a certain severity of morals, while laxity of morals seems to have spread among the middle and lower ranks. So the very families that were most profligate fifty years ago are now the most exemplary, and democracy seems only to have strengthened the morality of the aristocratic classes. The French Revolution divided the fortunes of the nobility, forced them to attend closely to their affairs and their families, made them live under the same roof as their children, and in short gave their minds a more rational and serious turn. In this way it gave them, almost without their realizing it, a reverence for religious belief, a love of order, of quiet pleasures, of domestic affection, and of comfort. The rest of the nation, which naturally had these same tastes, was swept into excesses by the effort needed to overthrow the country’s laws and political habits. The old French aristocracy has undergone the consequences of the Revolution, but it neither felt the revolutionary passions nor shared in the anarchic excitement that produced that crisis. It is easy to see that this aristocracy feels the salutary influence of the Revolution in its customs before those who carried it out. It may therefore be said, however paradoxical it first appears, that today the most anti-democratic classes of the nation are the ones chiefly showing the kind of morality that one may reasonably expect from democracy. I cannot help thinking that when we have obtained all the effects of this democratic Revolution, and have got past the tumult it has caused, the observations that now hold true only of a few will gradually become true of the whole community.
